package_info.why_malicious: The xz package was compromised by a threat actor who gained maintainer access and inserted a sophisticated backdoor into versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. The malicious code enables remote code execution (RCE) via the SSH protocol by deploying a trojanized liblzma.o object file during installation, which is then loaded by SSH processes to intercept authentication and allow unauthorized remote access. This attack impacts a critical compression library used by many Linux distributions, posing a severe supply chain risk.

execution_context.file_location: build-to-host.m4, configure.ac, and Bash scripts in the xz source tarball (e.g., scripts/build-to-host.sh)
required_permissions: filesystem (write access to /usr/lib or equivalent library directories)
network (if build scripts attempt to fetch remote resources)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Custom m4 macro and Bash scripts embedded in the xz source tarball that, during the build process, unpack a concealed archive and deploy a malicious precompiled liblzma.o object file into the build output directory, replacing or supplementing the legitimate library object.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation-time, the build scripts execute custom macros and Bash commands to extract a hidden archive, write a malicious liblzma.o object file into the build output, and ensure it is linked into the final library, resulting in a trojanized compression library present on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The build process introduces a precompiled binary object (liblzma.o) that is not present in legitimate xz releases, and the scripts are obfuscated and undocumented, deviating from standard build procedures.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal xz build scripts should only compile source code into binaries and libraries, not inject or deploy precompiled object files with hidden functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom build steps may be used for optional features or platform-specific optimizations, but never for inserting undocumented, precompiled binaries into core libraries.
key_indicators: Presence of undocumented or obfuscated build scripts (e.g., build-to-host.m4, build-to-host.sh)
Deployment of a precompiled liblzma.o object file not generated from local source
liblzma.o with hash values not matching official releases
Build process steps not present in previous or legitimate versions

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when SSH is invoked and loads liblzma)
execution_context.file_location: /usr/lib/liblzma.so (or equivalent), containing the malicious liblzma.o object code loaded by SSH processes
required_permissions: process (injection into SSH process memory space)
network (to enable remote command execution via SSH)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious compiled code within liblzma.o that, when loaded by SSH daemons or clients, hooks into the authentication process and enables a hidden code path for remote code execution by the attacker, triggered via specially crafted SSH authentication requests.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when SSH loads the trojanized liblzma.so containing the malicious object code, the code hooks into the SSH authentication process, intercepts authentication data, and enables a covert channel for the attacker to execute arbitrary commands remotely via SSH, resulting in unauthorized system access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: liblzma.o is not expected to interact with SSH authentication or provide any code paths for remote command execution; its presence in the SSH process memory space is highly anomalous.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Compression libraries like liblzma should only handle data compression and decompression, never interact with authentication mechanisms or enable remote access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for a compression library to hook into SSH authentication or provide remote code execution capabilities.
key_indicators: liblzma.so or liblzma.o loaded by SSH processes
Code paths within liblzma enabling remote command execution via SSH protocol
Unexplained modifications to authentication flow in SSH when xz 5.6.0/5.6.1 is installed
liblzma object code with symbols or behaviors not present in official releases

attack_chain.action: Threat actor creates a fake GitHub account, establishes trust, and gains maintainer access to the xz project.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to modify and publish official xz releases

attack_chain.action: Threat actor publishes malicious xz releases (5.6.0, 5.6.1) containing obfuscated build scripts and a backdoored object file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victims download and install compromised xz source tarballs

attack_chain.action: During installation, the build scripts execute, unpacking and deploying the malicious liblzma.o object file into the build output.
attack_chain.leads_to: Trojanized liblzma library present on the victim system

attack_chain.action: When SSH is used, the trojanized liblzma.so is loaded by the SSH process, activating the malicious code path.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote code execution via SSH authentication backdoor

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected deployment of precompiled binary object files (liblzma.o) during xz package installation
Obfuscated or undocumented build scripts (e.g., build-to-host.m4, build-to-host.sh) present in xz source tarballs
Compression libraries (liblzma) being loaded by SSH processes
liblzma.so or liblzma.o containing code paths that enable remote code execution via SSH authentication
file_indicators: Presence of liblzma.o or liblzma.so with hash values not matching official xz releases
Modified or additional build scripts (build-to-host.m4, build-to-host.sh) in xz source tarballs for versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1
xz package versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 present on system
network_indicators: Unusual outbound SSH connections initiated by system processes not associated with legitimate user activity
Unexpected remote command execution events via SSH, especially on systems with xz 5.6.0 or 5.6.1 installed
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installation or presence of xz versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. Inspect build scripts in xz source tarballs for undocumented or obfuscated steps, such as the presence of build-to-host.m4 or build-to-host.sh. Check for the presence and hash of liblzma.o or liblzma.so in system library directories, comparing against known-good hashes from official releases. Audit SSH processes for unexpected loading of liblzma and for code paths enabling remote command execution. Alert if compression libraries interact with authentication or network processes, or if SSH authentication flow is modified.
